```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.align = "center",
  fig.retina = 2,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

The package ships six example datasets. Together they span three
clinical settings, several subgroup definitions, and three effect
measures (incidence-rate ratios (IRRs), odds ratios (ORs), and hazard
ratios (HRs)). This vignette is a visual tour of those tables through
contribution-adjusted meta-analysis (CAMS): what was studied, who the
subgroups are, how the numbers enter a fit, and the native forest plot
of that fit. The CAMS model itself is `vignette("cam")`. Incomplete
subgroup tables (single-subgroup trials) are
`vignette("single-subgroup-trials")`.

CAMS is fitted on the log scale (`yi`, `vi`). Use
`exponentiate = TRUE` only when reporting ratios. `forestplot()` is the
native forest for a CAMS fit (`plot()` is the contribution / bubble
plot). Default `type = "subgroups"` draws both subgroup blocks in one
figure.

```{r load}
library(interactmeta)
```

## Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis

`age` and `edss` come from a systematic review of treatment-effect
modifiers of immunotherapies in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis
(RRMS) (Heesen, Röver, Salem et al. 2024). Each row is one trial ×
subgroup estimate. The `treatment` column is the immunotherapy in that trial (for
example BG-12, fingolimod, natalizumab). Both tables are analysed here
as **log incidence-rate ratios**; `edss` documents relapse rate ratio
endpoints.

### Age: Younger versus Older

The question is whether the immunotherapy effect differs between the
source review's **Younger** and **Older** age strata. The package labels
those strata as `Younger` and `Older`; it does not record the numeric
age cut.

```{r age-data}
data(age)
head(age)
```

```{r age-escalc}
age_es <- escalc(measure = "IRR", yi = age$yi, vi = age$vi, data = age)
```

```{r age-escalc-print}
head(age_es)
```

`yi` and `vi` are already the log-rate estimate and its variance;
`measure = "IRR"` tags that scale for CAMS.

```{r age-fit, cache = TRUE}
fit_age <- cam(age_es, reference = "Younger")
```

```{r age-forest, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
forestplot(fit_age, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

Every trial reports both age strata. The forest is a complete Younger /
Older table under Bayesian CAMS.

### Disability: Lower versus Higher EDSS

The same review also splits trials by **EDSS** (Expanded Disability
Status Scale) into **Lower** and **Higher** strata. The numeric EDSS cut
is not stored on the dataset. `CONFIRM` appears as a single trial here
(with separate treatment rows); in `age` the BG-12 and copaxone CONFIRM
estimates are labelled `CONFIRM-B` and `CONFIRM-C`.

```{r edss-data}
data(edss)
head(edss[, c("trial", "subgroup", "n", "treatment", "yi")])
```

```{r edss-escalc}
edss_es <- escalc(measure = "IRR", yi = edss$yi, vi = edss$vi, data = edss)
```

```{r edss-es-print}
head(edss_es)
```

```{r edss-fit, cache = TRUE}
fit_edss <- cam(edss_es, reference = "Lower")
```

```{r edss-forest, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
forestplot(fit_edss, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

Same review and complete-table structure as `age`, with Lower versus
Higher EDSS as the subgroup split.

## COVID-19 therapies

Two World Health Organization (WHO) Rapid Evidence Appraisal for
COVID-19 Therapies (REACT) prospective meta-analyses are included as
**event counts**. They are not the same question: one is systemic
corticosteroids in critically ill patients, split by ventilation; the
other is interleukin-6 (IL-6) antagonists in hospitalized patients,
split by concomitant corticosteroid use. Mortality odds ratios are
built from the 2×2 counts.

### Corticosteroids and ventilation support

Sterne, Murthy et al. (2020) analysed systemic corticosteroids and
mortality among critically ill patients with COVID-19. In `steroids` the
ventilation subgroups are **IV** and **NIV** (invasive and non-invasive
support, as labelled). Treatments are hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, or
methylprednisolone, depending on the trial.

Some trials report only one ventilation subgroup (zero counts in the
other). Those empty rows are dropped before the odds-ratio calculation;
missing trial × subgroup cells are then filled with a large variance.
The fit uses frequentist CAMS. See
`vignette("single-subgroup-trials")`.

```{r steroids-data}
data(steroids)
head(steroids)
```

```{r steroids-escalc}
steroids_es <- escalc(
  measure = "OR",
  ai = treat.events,
  bi = treat.total - treat.events,
  ci = cont.events,
  di = cont.total - cont.events,
  data = steroids[steroids$n > 0, ]
)
```

```{r steroids-escalc-print}
head(steroids_es)
```

```{r steroids-fit}
fit_steroids <- cam(
  steroids_es,
  reference = "NIV",
  engine = "metafor"
)
```

```{r steroids-forest, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
forestplot(fit_steroids, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

The forest keeps the IV-only trials (CoDEX, DEXA-COVID 19, RECOVERY) in
the IV block; they do not contribute a within-trial contrast.

### IL-6 antagonists and concomitant corticosteroids

Sterne, Murthy et al. (2021) analysed IL-6 antagonists and mortality
among patients hospitalized for COVID-19. The subgroup is concomitant
corticosteroid use (`yes` / `no`), not ventilation. There is no
`treatment` column: the intervention is the IL-6 antagonist comparison
in that meta-analysis.

The `yes` / `no` rows with no patients are dropped before the
odds-ratio calculation, as in the corticosteroid example. ARCHITECTS
and ImmCoVA then contribute only concomitant corticosteroids (`yes`);
BACC-Bay contributes only `no`. Those empty cells are filled with a
large variance, the same missing-cell representation as `steroids`. The
fit uses frequentist CAMS. See `vignette("single-subgroup-trials")`.

```{r il6-data}
data(il6)
head(il6)
```

```{r il6-table}
table(il6$trial[il6$n > 0], il6$subgroup[il6$n > 0])
```

```{r il6-escalc}
il6_es <- escalc(
  measure = "OR",
  ai = treat.events,
  bi = treat.total - treat.events,
  ci = cont.events,
  di = cont.total - cont.events,
  data = il6[il6$n > 0, ]
)
```

```{r il6-escalc-print}
head(il6_es)
```

```{r il6-fit}
fit_il6 <- cam(il6_es, reference = "no", engine = "metafor")
```

```{r il6-forest, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6}
forestplot(fit_il6, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

The forest has single-subgroup trials in both directions: `yes`-only
and `no`-only rows, plus the complete trials.

## Non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: RESPIRE

RESPIRE 1 and RESPIRE 2 were replicate Phase III trials of
ciprofloxacin dry-powder inhalation (14-day on/off) versus pooled
placebo in non-cystic fibrosis (non-CF) bronchiectasis (De Soyza et
al. 2018; Aksamit et al. 2018). Both `respire_age` and `respire_sex`
are published **hazard ratios** for **time to first exacerbation**,
with age and sex as the two subgroup splits of the same endpoint.

The log HR and its variance are already stored (`yi`, `vi`), derived
from the published interval with `log_hr_from_ci()`. RESPIRE 1 uses
97.5% intervals and RESPIRE 2 uses 95.1% intervals; do not substitute
$z = 1.96$.

### Age: under 65 versus 65 and older

```{r respire-age-data}
data(respire_age)
respire_age[, c("trial", "subgroup", "n", "hr", "ci_level", "yi", "vi")]
```

```{r respire-age-escalc}
respire_age_es <- escalc(
  measure = "GEN",
  yi = respire_age$yi,
  vi = respire_age$vi,
  data = respire_age
)
```

```{r respire-age-fit, cache = TRUE}
fit_respire_age <- cam(respire_age_es, reference = "<65")
```

```{r respire-age-forest, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
forestplot(fit_respire_age, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

Two trials, a published hazard-ratio endpoint, and both age strata in
each trial.

### Sex: Male versus Female

Same trials, endpoint, and treatment comparison; the strata are
**Male** and **Female**.

```{r respire-sex-data}
data(respire_sex)
respire_sex[, c("trial", "subgroup", "n", "hr", "yi")]
```

```{r respire-sex-escalc}
respire_sex_es <- escalc(
  measure = "GEN",
  yi = respire_sex$yi,
  vi = respire_sex$vi,
  data = respire_sex
)
```

```{r respire-sex-fit, cache = TRUE}
fit_respire_sex <- cam(respire_sex_es, reference = "Male")
```

```{r respire-sex-forest, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
forestplot(fit_respire_sex, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

The same RESPIRE endpoint and trials, split by sex instead of age.

## Summary

| Dataset | Disease area | Subgroup | Outcome | Effect measure | What the CAMS example illustrates |
|------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|--------------|
| `age` | RRMS immunotherapies | Younger / Older | Rate (log IRR) | Incidence-rate ratio | complete table; Bayesian CAMS; age interaction |
| `edss` | RRMS immunotherapies | Lower / Higher EDSS | Relapse rate ratio | Incidence-rate ratio | complete table; alternative RRMS subgroup |
| `steroids` | Critically ill COVID-19 | IV / NIV ventilation | Mortality | Odds ratio from 2×2 counts | incomplete table; IV-only trials |
| `il6` | Hospitalized COVID-19 | Corticosteroid yes / no | Mortality | Odds ratio from 2×2 counts | incomplete table; single-subgroup trials in both directions |
| `respire_age` | Non-CF bronchiectasis | `<65` / `>=65` | Time to first exacerbation | Hazard ratio | HR endpoint; age subgroup |
| `respire_sex` | Non-CF bronchiectasis | Male / Female | Time to first exacerbation | Hazard ratio | HR endpoint; sex subgroup |

## References

Heesen C, Röver C, Salem S, et al. (2024). Treatment effect modifiers of immunotherapies for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *Mult Scler J Exp Transl Clin*, 10(4), 20552173241274618.

WHO Rapid Evidence Appraisal for COVID-19 Therapies (REACT) Working Group, Sterne JAC, Murthy S, et al. (2020). Association between administration of systemic corticosteroids and mortality among critically ill patients with COVID-19: a meta-analysis. *JAMA*, 324(13), 1330--1341.

WHO Rapid Evidence Appraisal for COVID-19 Therapies (REACT) Working Group, Sterne JAC, Murthy S, et al. (2021). Association between administration of IL-6 antagonists and mortality among patients hospitalized for COVID-19: a meta-analysis. *JAMA*, 326(6), 499--518.

De Soyza A, Aksamit T, Bandel T-J, et al. (2018). RESPIRE 1: a phase III placebo-controlled randomised trial of ciprofloxacin dry powder for inhalation in non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis. *Eur Respir J*, 51(1), 1702052.

Aksamit T, De Soyza A, Bandel T-J, et al. (2018). RESPIRE 2: a phase III placebo-controlled randomised trial of ciprofloxacin dry powder for inhalation in non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis. *Eur Respir J*, 51(1), 1702053.

Panaro RV, Röver C, Friede T (2025). *Consistent Bayesian meta-analysis on subgroup specific effects and interactions.* arXiv:2512.18785.
